Xi-Trump-Putin summit: a 250-word “peace declaration” on nuclear weapons, oil and the UN, but nothing on Ukraine

On Thursday, November 19, in Shenzhen, Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin held their first three-way summit, lasting about 90 minutes on the sidelines of APEC. They signed a short four-point declaration: UN reform, higher oil production, criticism of the International Criminal Court and rejection of nuclear war [1][2][3].
The text is titled “Declaration of the Heads of State of China, Russia and the United States for Peace” [4]. It is about 250 words long [3][10].

On nuclear weapons, the three powers “reaffirm that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought” and promise a dialogue on risk reduction and non-proliferation, with no timetable [1]. The text mentions neither inspections nor cuts to weapons stockpiles [10].
On energy, the three countries say they want to work together to increase the production and supply of oil and refined products, a commitment that remains general [3].

The most discussed passage targets the International Criminal Court (ICC): it is surprising, since Vladimir Putin is himself the subject of an arrest warrant from that court [2][5]. On the UN, the text stays vague: no specific content for the reforms and no timetable [5].
The war with Iran was barely discussed: Donald Trump only repeated that Tehran could not have nuclear weapons [2]. He also asked Xi Jinping to help end the war in Ukraine [2].

The leaders piled on superlatives: “We are really making history,” Donald Trump said; Vladimir Putin described the talks as “open,” “free” and “useful” [10]. Xi Jinping called the meeting “revolutionary,” according to Chinese television CCTV [3].

On the same day, APEC's 21 economies adopted their final declaration by consensus, and Xi Jinping announced $20 million for APEC cooperation and a research center on the Asia-Pacific community in Shenzhen [8][9].

Key takeaway: the summit is historic in form but thin on substance. The only concrete promise, a dialogue on nuclear risks, has no date, and the declaration contains no plan for a disarmament treaty, which Donald Trump had long been calling for [1][6].

For Ukraine, nothing is settled. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha welcomed the fact that Shenzhen did not turn into the “Yalta Putin dreams of,” a reference to the 1945 conference where the great powers divided up Europe [6]. From Shenzhen, Vladimir Putin said he had invited the Europeans to Moscow to then set the format of negotiations [7].

Each leaves with something: Vladimir Putin breaks out of his isolation, Xi Jinping positions himself as host to the great powers, and Donald Trump, who lost control of Congress in the November midterm elections, can tout a diplomatic success [10][6].

This summit doesn't change your daily life right away. But the promise to pump more oil, if it materializes, could weigh on prices at the pump. And Europe's absence from this table shows that major decisions on Ukraine, which affect security and energy in France, are also being made without it.

Iran: Trump puts off any decision on new strikes until 2027, while Tehran says it blew up two supertankers in Hormuz

On the plane back from China on Thursday, November 19, Donald Trump told Reuters he would not decide on new strikes against Iran before early 2027. The same day, the Revolutionary Guards claimed that two supertankers had hit mines in Hormuz. Brent, meanwhile, barely moved, at $91.98 [1][4][6].

Asked by Reuters about new strikes, Donald Trump replied: “I'll talk to you about it after the start of the year,” adding “we have time” [1][3]. To Fox News, he said: “We'll see what happens after January 1”; to Axios and Israeli channel News 12: “I'm not rushing into any decision on Iran” [3].

It is a change of tone: before the November 3 congressional elections, he had suggested that Iran would be more inclined to make a deal after the vote [1]. He still repeats that he will act to prevent Tehran from getting nuclear weapons [1].

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pushing to resume the war as soon as possible, according to Axios; according to Reuters, he sent an envoy to argue for new strikes [3]. A US official believes, on the contrary, that economic pressure on Iran is enough for now [2].

On Thursday, the Revolutionary Guards navy claimed that two supertankers carrying more than 4 million barrels had struck a mine while taking an “unauthorized” route and were burning near the southern coast of the strait [6]. No independent source has confirmed this, and strong doubts surround these repeated announcements [7].

On the markets, a barrel of Brent closed Thursday up 3 cents at $91.98, and US WTI crude at $83.21, its lowest since August 26 [4]. On Friday morning, Brent rose to $92.22 but was still on track for a weekly drop of about 3.5%, its third in a row [4][5].

Key takeaway: by pushing his decision back to January, Donald Trump rules out, at least for a few weeks, a resumption of massive bombing against Iran, which removes a risk of an oil price spike [1][3].

The oil market barely reacts anymore to Iranian announcements of ships being hit. The reason: the International Energy Agency (IEA) estimates that global oil supply rose back above demand in October, and this fear of a surplus weighs more heavily than the incidents in Hormuz [4][5].

The Strait of Hormuz nevertheless remains a chokepoint: flows leaving the Persian Gulf are still below their pre-war level, according to tanker tracking [5]. Iran is using mines and threats to put pressure on the United States and its blockade [7].
The tug-of-war is also playing out in Washington: Benjamin Netanyahu wants swift strikes, and Donald Trump is keeping all options open [2][3].

Brent at around $92, down for three weeks, is rather good news for your fuel fill-ups and your heating oil bill, with a lag of a few weeks. But Trump's decision in January could change everything: if strikes resume, oil could climb back quickly.

Wall Street drops more than 2% and the Dow falls below 50,000 points, on the day Anthropic gains 17% in its Nasdaq debut

On Thursday, November 19, Wall Street's three major indexes fell at least 2%: the Dow Jones lost about 1,100 points and the Nasdaq 2.3%. The same day, Anthropic, creator of the Claude AI, ended its first trading session at $97.17, 17% above its IPO price of $83 [1][2][6].
Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, 34% above the IPO price, rose as high as $115 (+38.6%), then fell back to finish up 17.1% [1][5][7]. The stock trades under the ticker ANT [5].
The $83 price had been set on Wednesday evening, above the $70 to $78 range offered to investors [1]. The company raised $81.3 billion, the largest IPO in history [5].
Its value briefly topped $2 trillion during the session [1]. At the close, CNN put it at $1.76 trillion, counting all the shares that may be created (options, free shares for employees) [4].

The rest of the market plunged: the S&P 500, the index of the 500 largest US companies, lost about 2% for its sixth straight decline, its longest losing streak since 2024, and now stands 8.2% below its record from last month [2][1].
The Dow Jones fell 2.19% to 49,097.06 points, its first close below 50,000 since June; the Nasdaq Composite lost 550.69 points (2.3%) to 23,879.20 [3][2].
Nvidia posted a sixth straight session of losses, and chipmakers Micron and Broadcom also fell [1]. Alphabet, Google's parent company and an Anthropic shareholder, also declined [3].
The VIX, the “fear index” that measures expected market nervousness, jumped 15.8% to 28.44 [2][8].
Key takeaway: the largest IPO in history was a success for Anthropic, but it was not enough to rekindle enthusiasm for AI, which has been running out of steam on Wall Street for weeks [1].

How it works: to buy Anthropic shares, many funds sold other tech stocks. “That money is coming from somewhere,” says Jed Ellerbroek, a portfolio manager at Argent Capital, who cautions against drawing too many conclusions from the session, while acknowledging that his own enthusiasm for AI has waned [1].
The doubts concern the cost of AI investments and how they are financed: even Nvidia's very strong results released on Wednesday failed to revive its stock [1][8].
A 2% drop in a single session across all three indexes at once is still rare: it signals that the correction is no longer hitting only tech giants but the entire US market [2][3].

If you have a “world” or “S&P 500” ETF in your PEA or life insurance policy, it probably fell on Thursday, because US stocks weigh heavily in it. As for Anthropic, the stock can't be bought in a PEA, and a highly publicized IPO is never a guarantee of gains.

2027 budget: rejected by MPs, the bill reaches the Senate this Friday, and the government vows the 5% deficit is “not negotiable”

On Friday, November 20, the Senate begins examining the 2027 state budget, which the National Assembly rejected on November 4. Senators are therefore starting again from the government's original bill. It targets a public deficit of 5% of the wealth produced in 2027, and the government is already preparing a compromise with the parties [1][2][4].

The National Assembly rejected the 2027 finance bill (PLF, the state budget) on November 4: the Senate is therefore taking up the government's original version, without the changes voted by MPs [2][7].

The timetable: the first part, on revenue (taxes and levies), is being debated from Friday, November 20 to Saturday, November 28 or Sunday, November 29 [1]. The whole debate is due to last until December 9 [5].

The general rapporteur, Christine Lavarde (Les Républicains), got some sixty amendments on the revenue part adopted in committee [5]. In particular, she proposes scrapping the 10% allowance that retirees get on their taxable pensions [9].
The finance committee takes a harsh view of the government's strategy: according to it, the recovery of public finances has “stalled” [3].

The government is targeting a deficit of 5% of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2027, compared with 5.4% targeted for 2026 [4]. Economy Minister Roland Lescure considers the 1% growth forecast “at risk,” and calls the 5% “not negotiable” [4].

Before the senators, David Amiel, Minister for Public Action and Accounts, announced that Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu will list “in the coming days” the “priority topics for discussion” with a view to a compromise, while “holding to a framework, that of a 5% public deficit” [4].

Other Senate proposals affect civil servants, with cuts to the family pay supplement and therapeutic part-time work [6], and broadcasting: keeping Canal+'s reduced VAT rate and a heavier tax on video platforms' advertising [7].

Key takeaway: with no majority in the National Assembly, the government is counting on the Senate, dominated by the right and center, to move forward, and then on a compromise negotiated with the parties [1][4].

The public deficit is the gap between what the state, Social Security and local authorities spend and what they take in. It is expressed as a % of GDP, the wealth produced in the country in one year. Targeting 5% in 2027 means narrowing the gap by 0.4 points in one year [4].
The risk comes from growth: if the economy grows less than the forecast 1%, tax revenue comes in weaker and other savings must be found to meet the target, hence Roland Lescure's warning [4].
The Social Security budget, examined just before, shows the difficulty: the Senate adopted it on November 18 with a deficit of €14 billion, above the €12.7 billion targeted by the government [8].

If you're retired, keep an eye on the 10% allowance: scrapping it would raise your taxable income, and therefore potentially your tax [9]. If you're a civil servant with children, the family supplement is also on the table [6]. Nothing has been voted yet: the bill must then reach an agreement with MPs.

news.2026-11-20-ukraine-berlin-coalition: Ukraine: in Berlin, Trump's envoys see a “very united” Europe, but the Kremlin denies promising it a seat at the table

On Thursday, November 19, some thirty countries from the “coalition of the willing” met at the Chancellery in Berlin with Volodymyr Zelensky and, for the first time, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. On the agenda: security guarantees for Ukraine after a ceasefire, and its reconstruction [1][4][8].

The coalition of the willing, launched by Emmanuel Macron and Keir Starmer, brought together some thirty countries according to France 24; counts vary from 34 to about 40 delegations depending on the media outlet [1][5]. The European negotiating team, EU institutions and NATO sat down for the first time with Ukrainian and US negotiators [2].

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz repeated that the war would only end through diplomacy, and that Ukraine must keep its territorial integrity, obtain solid security guarantees and be anchored in European security [6]. He wants to negotiate “as a team” with Kyiv and Washington, with no “surprises” from Washington [7].
Volodymyr Zelensky said he doubted that Ukraine and its partners understand guarantees modeled on NATO's Article 5, the mutual defense clause, in the same way [5].

Jared Kushner described a Europe that is “very united, and very, very strong in its support for Ukraine,” a message passed on to Donald Trump [2]. Donald Trump, still on his plane back from China, joined the meeting remotely to recount his exchanges with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping [2][7].

Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff say Russia has agreed that Europe should have a seat at the next negotiations; Yuri Ushakov, the Kremlin's foreign policy adviser, denies any such agreement and says no date has been set for the next round [2][3].
From Shenzhen, Vladimir Putin said he had proposed that the Europeans come to Moscow, wanting first to know what they would bring before deciding on the format of the talks [9].
Key takeaway: for the first time, Washington, Kyiv and Europe discussed the post-war period together, but Moscow still refuses to grant the Europeans a seat in the negotiations [2][3].

The heart of the matter is security guarantees: what would stop Russia from attacking again after a ceasefire. The United States is offering guarantees similar to NATO's Articles 4 and 5, but bilateral and without US troops on the ground, which leaves Kyiv skeptical [5].

The meeting took place on the same day as the Shenzhen summit, and many feared that Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping would decide Ukraine's fate without it [4]. In the end, the Shenzhen declaration settled nothing on the war [1].

What happens next depends on a format that is still unclear: Volodymyr Zelensky is to discuss separately with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner the timetable and format of the next round, which Kyiv wants to expand to include Europe alongside the United States and Russia [3].

France is at the forefront of the coalition of the willing: security guarantees could one day involve French troops or additional defense spending, and therefore the state budget. And a lasting peace in Ukraine would affect the energy and wheat prices you pay.

EU–UK summit: the Twenty-Seven give their green light overnight, but Andy Burnham still threatens to walk away without a deal

On Friday, November 20, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham meets António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels for the second EU–UK summit. EU countries approved a package of agreements on food, carbon and youth mobility on Thursday evening, but London has not yet said yes [1][2][3].

The summit brings together António Costa, President of the European Council, Ursula von der Leyen, President of the Commission, and Andy Burnham. It is the second of its kind, after the one in London in May 2025 [1].
Three agreements are expected: less paperwork for exporting food, a link between the carbon markets on both sides, and a youth program [2].
Member states gave their green light to the package late on Thursday evening, according to several diplomats, but the final sign-off on the British side was still missing [2].
Downing Street speaks of talks going “down to the wire,” and Andy Burnham says he is ready to walk away without a deal if it is not in the UK's interest [3].

The main sticking point: university fees for European students in the UK [2]. The draft declaration offers two options: equal treatment with British students or “significantly reduced” fees for undergraduate degrees [4].
The text also plans to conclude in 2027 the negotiations on the UK joining the European electricity market [4]. The link between the carbon markets, however, has no implementation date [4].
On food rules, the two sides still disagreed the day before on London's role in drafting future European standards [2].
Key takeaway: London and Brussels are moving closer through small, concrete steps, without a return to the single market [2][4].
The carbon market (ETS) requires manufacturers to buy “pollution permits” for each tonne of CO2. Linking the two systems would avoid border carbon taxes on trade between the EU and the UK [4].

Food health rules (SPS) are at the heart of the checks that have slowed down trucks since Brexit. Aligning with European standards eases these checks, but London wants a say in future rules, which the EU is reluctant to grant [2].
For the youth program, the British government promises a time-limited, capped scheme, with no access to welfare benefits or the right to bring family members [5].

If you're between 18 and 30, this is the issue to watch: a deal would reopen the door to stays to study or work in the UK, and could lower the university fees paid by European students. For French companies that sell to the UK, fewer food checks mean lower costs.

AI chips: Washington approved nearly 880,000 Nvidia and AMD chips for China in six months, more than 30% of them for military-linked groups, Congress reveals

On Thursday, November 19, the House Foreign Affairs Committee published the export licenses granted by the Commerce Department: 879,868 Nvidia and AMD AI chips approved for Chinese buyers between December 2025 and May 2026, more than 30% of them for companies the Pentagon links to the Chinese military [1][2][3].
The documents come from the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), the Commerce Department agency that issues authorizations to export sensitive technologies [1][3].
The applications covered about 3.4 million chips; just over 879,000 were approved, notably for Chinese internet giants Alibaba and Tencent [3][4].
They are mainly Nvidia's H200 chips and their AMD equivalents, such as the MI325X: accelerators, the components that power the training and use of artificial intelligence models [2][3].

More than 30% of the approved chips were destined for companies the Pentagon links to the Chinese military [2]. Committee Chairman Brian Mast also claims that Nvidia applications named two companies he suspects of serving as fronts for smuggling [1].
Gregory Meeks, the committee's top Democrat, criticized the Trump administration's handling of export controls [3].
Nvidia says it complied with the Commerce Department rules in force at the time; AMD says its companies comply with US export laws [1][3].
The documents do not say how many of these chips actually reached China [2]. For Stacy Rasgon, an analyst at Bernstein, 879,000 chips is “not that many,” and the news is not surprising [1].

Key takeaway: for the first time, we can see in black and white how many US AI chips were approved for China, at the heart of the technological rivalry between the two countries, and that a significant share went to groups linked to the Chinese military [1][2].

How it works: to sell its most powerful AI chips in China, a US company must obtain a license from the BIS, which examines each application and can say yes or no [1][3]. Here, about a quarter of the chips requested were approved [3][4]. Publishing these licenses allows Congress to assess how the administration applies its own rules.

The political context matters: the committee is publishing these figures as Congress pushes to tighten restrictions on AI chips sold to China [3]. Allegations of shell companies used for smuggling fuel this debate [1].
For Nvidia and AMD, the stakes are twofold: China remains an outlet, but each new restriction can shrink it. Analysts, such as those at Bernstein, nevertheless play down the volumes at stake [1].

AI chips have become as much a security issue as a trade one. If Congress secures a crackdown, Nvidia and AMD could lose part of the Chinese market: a topic that matters if your savings (life insurance, equity savings plan) are invested in US or tech stock funds.

Rohingya: for the first time, the UN's highest court finds a state guilty of genocide, Myanmar

On Thursday, November 19, in The Hague, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the UN court that rules on disputes between states, concluded that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya, a Muslim minority, in 2017. It is the first time a state has been held responsible for genocide before this court [1][2].

The case had been brought by the Gambia, a small West African country, under the 1948 Genocide Convention [2][5]. The judges found three types of acts committed by Myanmar's security forces: killings, serious bodily or mental harm, and measures intended to prevent births [5].
The court said it was “fully convinced” that Myanmar had acted with the intent to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya group, an essential condition for genocide [5].
The presiding judge, Iwasawa Yuji of Japan, explained that “the scale and nature of the atrocities” were characteristic of an intent to destroy a substantial part of the group [1][3].
Myanmar argued that its operations targeted Rohingya insurgents; the court rejected this defense, finding that the army did not distinguish between combatants and civilians [3].
On one point, the Gambia failed to convince: the judges did not uphold public incitement to genocide by private actors [5].
The court orders Myanmar to cease all violence, investigate those responsible and pay “adequate, effective and prompt” reparation to the Rohingya, as a group and individually [4][5].
At the time of the first reports, Myanmar's military-backed government had not reacted [3]. A US official told Al Jazeera that Washington was studying the consequences of the ruling [2].
Key takeaway: this is a historic ruling, the first in which the UN's highest court declares a state fully responsible for genocide within the meaning of the 1948 convention [1][6].

But the ICJ has no police force to enforce its rulings [4]. The Gambia can take the case to the UN Security Council and ask it to act [4]. The judgment also orders reparations for the victims, which opens a long legal process [4][5].

The judgment weighs on Myanmar's junta just as it seeks to break out of its isolation: its leader, Min Aung Hlaing, now president, was still kept away from the Southeast Asian (ASEAN) summit in Manila last week. Before the verdict, Myanmar denied any genocide [3].
The 2017 violence was committed by the army, the same one that seized power and now runs the country: in theory, it is the army that will have to investigate its own crimes [3][4].

What about me? This ruling by the UN's highest court sets a precedent: it is the first time a state has been found responsible for genocide [1]. It could support European countries, including France, when they discuss sanctions against Myanmar's junta or the reception of Rohingya refugees.

On Thursday, November 19, in Berlin, at the summit of the “coalition of the willing” supporting Ukraine, Emmanuel Macron called for “reopening the question” of Kyiv joining NATO. Canada: Ottawa aims for an “interim” deal with Trump by the end of December, while his adviser Navarro compares Canadian negotiators to a high school team

Canada wants to conclude an interim agreement with the United States by the end of December to ease tariffs on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber, according to CBC. On Thursday, November 19, Trump adviser Peter Navarro accused Ottawa of “arrogance”; Mark Carney replied that, without a deal, Canada is “busy” elsewhere [1][3][5].

According to members of the federal advisory council on Canada-US relations, which met on Thursday with Minister Dominic LeBlanc, Ottawa is first aiming for an “interim,” meaning temporary, arrangement by the end of the year [1][2].

It would cover the “232” tariffs (a section of US law on national security) that hit steel, aluminum, autos and softwood lumber, as well as the “338” tariffs imposed in August, after talks broke down [1].

Dominic LeBlanc warns that some of the “232” tariffs would remain, at lower rates: Canada will not get to zero US tariffs [1][7]. The deal would mainly serve to launch the official review of CUSMA, the North American free trade agreement [1].
In Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the APEC summit, Mark Carney said a “very good trade arrangement” was possible after meeting Donald Trump and his team, including Jamieson Greer and Marco Rubio [4].

“This should have been done six months ago, but we are not going to sign something that doesn't make sense for Canada,” said the Prime Minister, who is demanding “a viable Canadian auto sector” [4]. He added: “If the United States doesn't want a deal, we're busy” [3].

That same Thursday, Peter Navarro, Trump's trade adviser, accused Ottawa of “arrogance and dishonesty”: Canadian negotiators are “like a high school team up against the New York Knicks. It doesn't end well for Canada” [5].
On Tuesday, Navarro had already called out Carney, who had raised the idea of a bigger role for China in the Canadian auto industry [5][6].

Key takeaway: Ottawa is scaling back its ambitions. Rather than a major agreement, it is seeking a first step by the end of December to provide relief for steel, aluminum, autos and lumber, even if that means keeping reduced tariffs [1][7].

The context: in July, Washington refused to extend the North American agreement. A month later, Carney rejected a draft deemed a threat to Canada's sovereignty and retaliated with tariffs on US products [5].

How it works: a tariff is a tax paid on imports. The “232” tariffs target entire sectors in the name of national security. An interim deal can lower them quickly, without waiting for the full renegotiation of CUSMA, which would only start afterward [1].

The signals are mixed: Carney points out that Canada is diversifying its partners, while Navarro applies pressure in public [3][5]. For Ottawa, the challenge is to sign without appearing to give in, with autos remaining the sticking point [4].

For you, this is a good indicator of how Washington treats its allies on trade. A deal that reduces US tariffs without eliminating them would show they are here to stay on steel, aluminum and autos, sectors where Europe also exports to the United States.

Brazil: the central bank sells $1 billion to support the real, a first since 2024, and Lula accuses markets of “speculation”

On Thursday, November 19, the Central Bank of Brazil sold $1 billion on the spot market to curb the real's slide, its first intervention of this kind since December 2024. The dollar nevertheless ended at 5.93 reais, its highest since April 2025, on the day Lula lashed out at “speculators” [1][2][4].

The operation lasted five minutes, from 12:03 to 12:08 p.m. Brasília time, after the dollar climbed as high as 5.9287 reais [2]. The central bank accepted five bids, at a rate of 5.86 reais to the dollar [3].
The dollar first fell back, then rose again and closed up about 1.1% at 5.93 reais, its highest level since April 2025 [2][3].

According to Bloomberg, the central bank is seeking to stem a drop of about 15% in the real since Lula's re-election in October [1]. The day after the vote, the real had lost more than 11% against the dollar during the session and the São Paulo stock exchange (Bovespa index) had closed down 13.9% [5].

The same day, in Brasília, Lula accused market players of profiting from “speculation” and rumors about the makeup of his future government [4]. He says he has not discussed it and is in no hurry: “I will appoint each minister when I want to” [4].

Re-elected in October for a fourth, non-consecutive term against right-wing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula begins his new term in January; on Wednesday, the Senate approved his savings plan, which investors see as merely a first step in the face of worsening debt [4].

Key takeaway: despite a $1 billion intervention, the central bank failed to lift the real, which ended the day at its lowest since April 2025 [1][2]. Markets want assurances on public finances, not just a one-off intervention [4].

How it works: in a “spot” sale, the central bank draws on its reserves and sells dollars to banks, for immediate delivery. More dollars available on the market should, in principle, mean a cheaper dollar and a stronger real [1][3]. But if investors keep selling reais, the effect quickly fades, as it did on Thursday [2].

The crux is fiscal confidence. As early as October, Graham Stock of asset manager RBC BlueBay said the key signal for markets would be the next Lula government's commitment to fiscal discipline, starting with the choice of a new finance minister [5]. By refusing to reveal his choices, Lula is keeping markets waiting [4].
A weak real makes imported goods more expensive, and therefore the prices Brazilians pay, and increases the burden of dollar debts: the central bank cannot let it slide without reacting.

If you travel to Brazil, your euro goes further than it did a few months ago. If you have “emerging markets” funds in your life insurance policy, Brazil often carries significant weight in them: the fall of the real and of the São Paulo stock exchange since October may show up in their performance.

Senegal: Sonko's MPs bury the 2027 budget, President Faye forces it through by decree, and the IMF loan wobbles

On Wednesday, November 18, Senegal's National Assembly, dominated by Ousmane Sonko's Pastef party, rejected the 2027 budget. On Thursday, November 19, President Bassirou Diomaye Faye hit back by putting into effect by decree the 2026 amended budget, which MPs had already rejected. A $2.2 billion IMF program is at stake [1][2][3].
MPs rejected, by 126 votes to 18, the first part of the 2027 budget, which sets revenue, authorized spending and borrowing [4][5]. Without it, the second part cannot even be debated [5].
The bill provided for 5,653.9 billion CFA francs in revenue and 7,005.6 billion in spending, a deficit of 1,351.7 billion [5].

On November 19, through decree No. 2026-2416, the president put into effect the 2026 amended finance law, rejected by the Assembly on November 3 [5]. His office says he is acting as “guardian of the Constitution” and guarantor of the “regular functioning of the state” [2]. MP Amadou Ba disputes this right [5].

Pastef lawmakers call the forecasts “not credible,” because they are based on the 2026 budget they had rejected [4]. Finance Minister Cheikh Diba warns that social programs and investments could be delayed [1].

The conflict pits two former allies against each other: Faye dismissed Sonko as Prime Minister in May, and Sonko became Speaker of the Assembly a few days later [1][6]. On November 17, Pastef expelled President Faye and 31 other members [7].
The IMF and Senegal have agreed on a program of about $2.2 billion over 36 months, but the Fund's executive board has not yet approved it [3].

Key takeaway: Senegal is mired in a debt crisis, and the IMF program is the key to its strategy for restructuring it. But this program requires voted budgets: the standoff between Faye and Sonko is blocking it [1][3].
Governing by decree makes it possible to pay civil servants and keep spending, but it undermines the legitimacy of the public accounts in the eyes of creditors, who want solid commitments [3][5].

What comes next could be a dissolution of the Assembly: according to one analyst, the Constitution allows the president to dissolve it from December 2, which would lead to early legislative elections in the first quarter of 2027 [3]. Pastef, for its part, could try to bring down the government through a no-confidence motion [8].

The dispute has spilled beyond the budget into an open struggle between the presidency and Parliament, according to Reuters [1]. As long as the heads of the executive and the legislature are at odds, no reform required by the IMF can pass into law [3].

What about me? France is one of Senegal's leading partners, and many French companies operate there (banks, energy, construction). A political crisis that delays IMF aid can slow down projects and state payments, with effects on these companies and on the Senegalese diaspora in France [1][3].

Sudan: paramilitaries seize Bau and close in on Ed Damazin, capital of Blue Nile near Ethiopia

The Rapid Support Forces (RSF), paramilitaries at war with the Sudanese army since 2023, say they took the locality of Bau, in the Blue Nile region in the southeast of the country, on Thursday, November 19. They would thus control three of the region's seven localities. Thousands of residents are fleeing to Ed Damazin [1][2].

According to military sources cited by Sudan Tribune, the RSF entered Bau without a fight, after a large army force withdrew to Ed Damazin, the regional capital [1]. An RSF commander cited by Radio Tamazuj, on the contrary, speaks of an entry after clashes [2].

Both sides claim the nearby town of Derang, southwest of Ed Damazin, near the borders with Ethiopia and South Sudan [3]. The army says it destroyed 28 RSF combat vehicles there; the RSF claims to have taken Derang and the village of Al-Madina 12 and pursued the soldiers to the outskirts of Ed Damazin [3].

Here the RSF is fighting alongside its allies from the SPLM-N, a local rebel movement, within the Tasis alliance [2][3]. On November 3, this alliance had already taken the Sali military base, south of Ed Damazin [4].

More than 1,400 families have fled Geissan, Wad al-Mahi and Bau because of the fighting [5]. Between January and August, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) had already counted about 100,000 displaced people in Blue Nile [6].

On November 16, the army had announced the dispatch of five combat units to the headquarters of its 4th Infantry Division in Ed Damazin [7]. Its aircraft also struck the RSF headquarters in Nyala, capital of South Darfur [5].

The same day, a court in Port Sudan sentenced RSF leader Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as “Hemedti,” and 13 other commanders to death in absentia for looting the national medical supplies fund, a case estimated at $396 million. It is his second death sentence this year [8][9].
Key takeaway: Sudan's war is spreading to the southeast, on the border with Ethiopia, while the Horn of Africa is already under strain [1][7].

The RSF is closing in on Ed Damazin, where the army has gathered its reinforcements [1][7]. It already controls vast parts of Darfur, in the west [9]; a breakthrough in Blue Nile would give it a new border region.

The Sudanese government, based in Port Sudan, accuses Ethiopia of helping the RSF and the SPLM-N; the army says it shot down a drone coming from Ethiopia in the Dandro area [10]. Such involvement would widen the conflict to the entire region.

The sentences against Hemedti are mainly symbolic: the court asked to go through Interpol to obtain his extradition, but his whereabouts are unknown and he controls vast territories [9]. Both sides claim victories without independent verification [1][3].

What about me? Sudan is one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world: European aid, including France's, is at stake there. A war spilling over into Ethiopia would further weaken the Horn of Africa, close to the Red Sea, a route for part of the trade between Asia and Europe.

Guyana: a former US official suggested letting Venezuela have part of Essequibo, two-thirds of the country, Reuters reveals

According to a Reuters investigation published on Thursday, November 19, Jeremy Lewin, a former policy official at the US State Department, floated the idea of Venezuela taking partial control of Essequibo, a region covering the western two-thirds of Guyana. Washington says its position on the border has not changed [1][2][3].

Three people familiar with the matter described it to Reuters; two of them said Jeremy Lewin raised the idea of partial Venezuelan control over Essequibo [1]. The idea alarmed Guyanese officials, and Washington had to reassure them about its position [1].
Jeremy Lewin says he held “preliminary” discussions with the Guyanese and the Venezuelans, exchanges that were “entirely directed and authorized by the White House,” according to him [1].

It all reportedly started with a letter: in May, Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, allegedly wrote to Donald Trump to request US mediation for direct talks with Guyana [1]. Reuters was unable to verify the authenticity of this letter [1]. Lewin says she raised the issue during their meeting in Caracas in July [1].

A State Department official replied that the administration receives ideas and options from outside “every day,” but that its position on the border between Venezuela and Guyana has not changed [1][2].

After publication, Guyana's Foreign Ministry said the border dispute had been discussed with the State Department at a meeting in September, with the focus on the proceedings before the International Court of Justice (ICJ) [1][3].
The governments of Guyana and Venezuela had not responded to Reuters' numerous requests before publication [1].

The revelation comes the day after an unprecedented visit: on Wednesday, November 18, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Delcy Rodríguez in Caracas and signed a military cooperation agreement, the first visit by a Pentagon chief to Venezuela since the turn of the century [4].

Key takeaway: even though Washington denies any change, the mere fact that a US official raised the idea of dividing Essequibo worries Guyana, which is relying on international justice to defend its border [1][3].

The context: Delcy Rodríguez has led Venezuela since US special forces captured Nicolás Maduro in early January [4]. Since then, Caracas and Washington have grown closer, culminating in the military agreement against the cartels signed this week [4]. Guyana fears it will pay the price for this rapprochement.

How it works: the International Court of Justice, based in The Hague, is the UN court that settles disputes between states. Guyana wants the border to be set by it [3]. A direct discussion with Caracas under US auspices would bypass this framework, which explains the concern in Georgetown, the Guyanese capital [1].
For the Trump administration, the balance is delicate: reassuring Guyana while now working with Caracas on defense and the fight against the cartels [1][4].

It's far from home, but it's a reminder that borders can become negotiable again when a great power gets involved. Venezuela is an oil country: any tension in the region is closely watched by energy markets, which set the price of your fill-up.

news.2026-11-20-riyad-tour-pif-houthis.s: On Thursday, November 19, the Public Investment Fund (PIF) tower, Riyadh's tallest skyscraper and headquarters of the Saudi sovereign wealth fund, was damaged by a strike attributed to Yemen's Houthi rebels. No one was injured, but windows were blown out on seven to eight floors. Riyadh reserves the right to take “all necessary measures” [1][2][3].
news.2026-11-20-riyad-tour-pif-houthis.p: Saudi civil defense reported material damage on several floors of the building and on neighboring buildings, with no injuries [2]. According to Reuters, the strike destroyed windows on seven to eight floors and twisted part of the metal facade [2].
Official statements do not name the building, but photos clearly show the PIF tower; three sources familiar with the matter told Reuters that a Houthi missile had hit it directly [2][3].

The Saudi Foreign Ministry condemned “continued terrorist attacks against civilian and economic facilities” in Riyadh, and reserved the right to take “all necessary measures” to defend its sovereignty, its citizens and its national assets [2][1].
Qatar, Kuwait and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), which groups six monarchies in the region, also condemned the attack [4].

Later in the day, the Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack: their military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said they had targeted King Khalid International Airport and Riyadh's financial center with cruise missiles [4].

It is not the first time: on November 8, the Houthis had already said they hit a building belonging to Aramco, the Saudi oil giant, in the same district, and they claim attacks on Riyadh airport on eight days in October and six in November [4].
news.2026-11-20-riyad-tour-pif-houthis.w: Key takeaway: by hitting the sovereign wealth fund's tower, the Houthis are striking the very symbol of Saudi Arabia's economic project, in the heart of Riyadh's financial district [3][5].

Saudi air defenses are no longer enough: at least 26 people have been killed by drones and missiles attributed to the Houthis in Saudi Arabia since September 23, according to the kingdom's authorities [6].

This campaign is part of the regional war around Iran, the Houthis' ally: since the summer, they have also been targeting Saudi oil facilities, including the East-West pipeline that allows the kingdom to export without going through the Strait of Hormuz [7].
The Saudi response is the big unknown: by reserving “all necessary measures,” Riyadh is raising the threat of retaliation in Yemen, which would further widen the conflict [2].

El Salvador: Nayib Bukele runs for a third consecutive term, a first, after sending his soldiers to fight gangs in Haiti

On Thursday, November 19, El Salvador's president, Nayib Bukele, registered his candidacy for the February 2027 presidential election to seek a third consecutive term, something unprecedented in the country. The clear favorite, he is running alongside his vice president Félix Ulloa; the opposition and international observers consider the candidacy illegal [2][3][4].
Nayib Bukele filed his candidacy on Thursday for the February 2027 vote, once again with Vice President Félix Ulloa at his side [2]. He is the clear favorite [2].
Facing him: Maytee Iraheta of the Nationalist Republican Alliance (ARENA, right) and Rafael Aguirre of the Farabundo Martí National Liberation Front (FMLN, left) [2].
The legal path is contested: in 2021, the Supreme Court struck down the rule that prevented a president from running again, which allowed Bukele to seek a second term in 2024 [2][4].
In 2025, the Legislative Assembly adopted a constitutional reform that allows him to run a third time and extends the presidential term from five to six years [2][4].
Opponents and international observers consider the candidacy illegal, but cannot deny the president's popularity; the government rejects the idea that these changes weaken checks and balances [2].

Bukele is also exporting his fight against gangs: he has deployed about 2,500 soldiers to Haiti, according to the AP news agency, after four Salvadoran aviation technicians disappeared during a gang attack in October [3]. Reuters puts the figure at more than 2,000 troops [1].

Key takeaway: Nayib Bukele is set to stay in power well beyond what the original Constitution allowed, thanks to a court ruling and then a reform passed by the Assembly [2][4]. With six-year terms, a victory in 2027 would keep him at the head of the country for a long time [2].

How it works: term limits are meant to prevent a leader from concentrating power for too long. “Checks and balances” are the institutions that can rein in the president: judges, Parliament, the press. The opposition believes they have been weakened; the government disputes this [2].

His popularity rests on the war against gangs, which he is now taking as far as Haiti, after the disappearance of four Salvadoran technicians [3]. By sending between 2,000 and 2,500 soldiers depending on the source, he is turning his security approach into a foreign policy argument [1][3].
The February 2027 vote will show whether the opposition, represented by ARENA and the FMLN, can still carry weight against a president who is the clear favorite [2].

For you, this is a textbook case of a debate running through many democracies: how far can a popular leader change the rules to stay in power? The answer from Salvadoran voters, in February 2027, will be watched across the region.

Fiji: El Niño dries out the archipelago, the government declares a state of national disaster and rations the capital's water every night

Fiji, a South Pacific archipelago, has declared a state of national disaster in the face of a drought linked to the El Niño climate phenomenon, which has reached “crisis” level. Water is cut off every night in the capital region, Suva. Neighboring Tonga has taken a similar measure [1][2][3].
The government approved the declaration on the advice of the National Disaster Risk Management Council; it is valid for one month and can be extended or lifted [1][4].
It grants exceptional powers: rationing water, evacuating residents and reallocating public funds [2]. The National Disaster Controller can organize population movements by land, sea or air [4].
Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka announced 20 million Fijian dollars (about 8.5 million US dollars), taken from existing funds, to secure water supplies for families and farmers [2].

The Water Authority of Fiji cuts off water every day from 9 p.m. to 4 a.m. in Greater Suva, to let reservoirs refill overnight: the Tamavua treatment plant has lost more than 15% of the raw water that feeds it [1][4].

The Fiji Meteorological Service forecasts below-normal rainfall from November to April, and above-normal temperatures until January [4]. The US Climate Prediction Center gives a more than 79% chance of a strong to very strong El Niño between January and March [2].
In early November, Rabuka had been criticized for downplaying the effects of El Niño [2]. In Tonga, drought had already been declared in October across all the main islands [5].
Key takeaway: small Pacific islands are on the front line of climate disruption. A drought lasting several months threatens families' drinking water and farmers' harvests [1][2].

El Niño is a natural warming of part of the Pacific Ocean that recurs every few years and shifts rainfall patterns: drought in the South Pacific and Southeast Asia, floods elsewhere. The Fiji Meteorological Service also expects above-normal heat [4].
The issue is also political: at the UN climate conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, Fiji's Climate Change Minister, Tabuya, rejected the draft final text: “We cannot accept it” [6].
With below-normal rainfall expected until April, the crisis could last the entire southern summer, and the one-month declaration will probably have to be extended [4].

What about me? France is also a Pacific power, with New Caledonia, French Polynesia and Wallis and Futuna, neighbors of Fiji exposed to the same El Niño. A strong El Niño, which US forecasters consider very likely, also affects the world's major agricultural regions, with possible effects on prices [2].

news.2026-11-20-asie-krach-ia-softbank.s: On Friday, November 20, Asian stock markets plunged in Wall Street's wake. Shares of Japan's SoftBank, a major OpenAI shareholder, fell more than 16%, Tokyo's Nikkei lost more than 4% and Seoul's Kospi nearly 5%. Taiwan is heading for its worst week since 1991 [1][2][4].
news.2026-11-20-asie-krach-ia-softbank.p: In Tokyo, SoftBank Group tumbled 16.16% on Friday, according to CNBC [1], to its lowest in seven months according to Investing.com [7]. The Nikkei 225 lost about 4.5% in the morning, dragged down by SoftBank, Advantest (chip testing) and Kioxia (memory) [8][9]. According to Reuters, the index was down 4.1% and heading for a 6.8% drop over the week [3].

In Seoul, the Kospi opened down 4.08% at 4,928.51 points [4], then was down 4.78% at 9:56 a.m., below the 4,900-point mark [5]. The day before, it had still gained 1.39%, ahead of Anthropic's debut [4]. Chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics were down about 6% and 4% early in the session [8].
Taiwan, the island of microchips, is the hardest hit: −5% on Friday and −16% over the week, its steepest weekly drop since 1991, according to Reuters [2].

The MSCI index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan lost 3.2% on the day and 8.3% over the week: the worst week since 2020 [2]. It fell to its lowest since early April, according to Investing.com [6].
It all started on Wall Street: on Thursday, the Dow Jones lost 1,101 points (−2.19%) and ended below 49,100 points, the Nasdaq fell 2.25% and the S&P 500 declined for the sixth straight session [12].
news.2026-11-20-asie-krach-ia-softbank.w: Key takeaway: Anthropic's stock market success did not reassure investors, quite the opposite. Its shares gained more than 30% in their debut, but that did not lift the rest of the AI sector, according to Reuters [2]. Investors are selling what they bought over the past months.

Reuters cites several concerns: Jensen Huang's departure from the helm of Nvidia, the debt piled up by the AI sector to build its data centers, and the prospect of rate hikes by the Fed, the US central bank [2]. When rates rise, risk-free investments pay more, and expensive stocks become less attractive.

Asia is on the front line because its stock markets are full of chip and memory makers that sell to US AI giants. When Wall Street doubts this spending, Taiwan, Seoul and Tokyo take the hit first [2][8].
news.2026-11-20-asie-krach-ia-softbank.f: If you have a world fund, a tech fund or life insurance invested in stocks, you inevitably hold some Asian chipmakers and AI giants. A week like this one lowers the displayed value. It only becomes a real loss if you sell at the bottom.
